title: If it rains on Saturday…
grammar: if + present: zero conditional (always) · first conditional (this time)

scene.speaker: ingrid
scene.bubble: Every good captain has a plan B. If it rains on Saturday, the picnic moves to the lighthouse!
scene.intro: Every good captain has a plan B. If it rains on Saturday, we'll do the quiz inside, says Ingrid, writing on the board. If it's sunny, we'll have the picnic by the lake and swim before lunch. If the bus is late, we'll walk. And if Kili delivers the invitations on time, everybody will come — which is the biggest 'if' of all. What will you do if it rains this weekend? Make your own plan A and plan B!

activities.title: Grammar · If it’s sunny, we go swimming
activities.instructions: Read the sentences. Then choose the right form.

data.title: Two kinds of if
data.intro: This unit is full of plans for next Saturday. But there is another if, the one for what is always true — and that is the one the Flyers exam asks for.
data.can: I can tell the two kinds of if apart: what always happens, and what we will do this time.

examples.text: If it’s sunny, we go swimming. — always, every sunny day.
If Kili smells biscuits, he comes to the window. It happens every time.
If it rains on Saturday, we’ll do the quiz inside. — just this Saturday.
If you open the door, the light comes on. Try it!

rules: Always true → present in both halves: If it’s sunny, we go swimming.
A plan for one day → present + will: If it rains, we’ll stay inside.
Either way, never put will after if. The will goes in the other half.
